questions.q: A runner completes one lap of a $400$ m track. Their displacement is:
questions.solution:
**Displacement** is the straight-line change in position, and the runner ends where they started — so it is **zero**.

The **distance** travelled is $400$ m. Displacement is a vector; distance is a scalar.

$\mathbf{v^{2} = u^{2} + 2as}$ contains no $t$ — which is exactly why it is useful when the time is neither known nor wanted.

All four hold only for **constant** acceleration.

questions.q: For a projectile with no air resistance, the horizontal velocity:
questions.solution:
With no air resistance there is no horizontal force, so the horizontal velocity is **constant** throughout.

Only the vertical component changes, under gravity. The two are entirely independent — which is why a bullet fired horizontally and one dropped at the same instant hit the ground together.

questions.q: Two objects of different mass are dropped in a vacuum. They:
questions.solution:
**The same rate.** A heavier object is pulled harder but has proportionally more inertia:

$a = \dfrac{F}{m} = \dfrac{mg}{m} = g$ — the mass cancels.

In air a feather falls slowly because of air resistance, not because of its mass, which the vacuum demonstration on the Moon settled for good.

questions.q: The area under a velocity-time graph gives:
questions.solution:
Area $=$ velocity $\times$ time $=$ **displacement**.

The **gradient** gives acceleration. Area below the axis counts as negative displacement, which is how a graph distinguishes displacement from distance.

questions.q: A car accelerates from rest at $3$ m/s$^{2}$ for $4$ s. Find its final velocity, in m/s.
An object starting from rest accelerates at $2$ m/s$^{2}$ for $5$ s. Find the distance travelled, in m.
An object is dropped from rest. Find its speed (in m/s) after falling $20$ m. Take $g = 10$ m/s$^{2}$.
questions.solution:
$v^{2} = u^{2} + 2as = 0 + 2(10)(20) = 400$, so $v = \mathbf{20}$ m/s.

Using the equation without $t$ avoids finding the time at all.

questions.q: A ball is thrown horizontally from a cliff $45$ m high. Find the time (in s) to reach the ground. Take $g = 10$ m/s$^{2}$.
questions.solution:
Consider the **vertical** motion alone: $u = 0$.

$45 = \tfrac12(10)t^{2} \Rightarrow t^{2} = 9 \Rightarrow t = \mathbf{3}$ s.

The horizontal speed has no effect on the time of fall — which is the whole point of independent components.

questions.q: A car travels $60$ m in $4$ s, accelerating uniformly from $10$ m/s. Find its final velocity, in m/s.
Derive the equation $s = ut + \tfrac12 at^{2}$ from a velocity-time graph, and state the assumption it depends on.
questions.solution:
**The graph.** For constant acceleration, the velocity-time graph is a **straight line** from $u$ at $t = 0$ to $v$ at time $t$.

**The displacement is the area** under it, which is a trapezium — or, more conveniently, a rectangle plus a triangle.

**Rectangle:** height $u$, width $t$, area $ut$. This is the distance that would have been covered at the original speed.

**Triangle:** base $t$, height $(v - u) = at$, area $\tfrac12 t(at) = \tfrac12 at^{2}$. This is the extra distance gained by accelerating.

**Total:**

$s = ut + \tfrac12 at^{2}$ ∎

**The assumption: the acceleration must be constant.** Otherwise the graph is not a straight line and the area is not a trapezium.

All four equations of motion share this restriction, and applying them to a car in real traffic, or to any motion with significant air resistance, is simply wrong.

**For non-uniform acceleration** the area is still the displacement — but it must be found by integration, $s = \displaystyle\int v\,dt$, of which this derivation is the simplest case.

questions.q: A ball is projected at $20$ m/s at $30°$ above the horizontal. Find the time of flight, the maximum height and the range. Take $g = 10$ m/s$^{2}$.
questions.solution:
**Resolve the initial velocity:**

$u_{x} = 20\cos 30° = 17.3$ m/s (constant throughout)

$u_{y} = 20\sin 30° = 10$ m/s

**Time to the top.** At the highest point the **vertical** velocity is zero:

$0 = 10 - 10t \Rightarrow t = 1$ s.

**Total time of flight** — the path is symmetrical, so it is twice that:

$T = \mathbf{2}$ s.

**Maximum height:**

$h = u_{y}t - \tfrac12 gt^{2} = 10(1) - 5(1) = \mathbf{5}$ m.

**Range** — horizontal velocity times total time:

$R = 17.3 \times 2 = \mathbf{34.6}$ m.

**The method throughout:** treat the two directions **separately**. Horizontally there is no acceleration, so distance is simply speed times time; vertically the motion is free fall with $u_{y}$ as the initial velocity.

**Two useful facts.** The horizontal velocity is never zero, even at the top — only the vertical one is. And the maximum range for a given speed occurs at $45°$, where $\sin 2\theta$ reaches 1.

questions.q: Describe how to obtain displacement, velocity and acceleration from one another using graphs, and sketch in words the three graphs for a ball thrown vertically upwards and caught again.
questions.solution:
**The relationships.**

• **Gradient** of a displacement-time graph $=$ velocity

• **Gradient** of a velocity-time graph $=$ acceleration

• **Area** under a velocity-time graph $=$ displacement

• **Area** under an acceleration-time graph $=$ change in velocity

Differentiating moves one way down the list; integrating moves back up.

**For a ball thrown up at $u$ and caught at the same height.**

**Displacement-time:** an inverted parabola. It rises, flattens at the top, and falls back to zero. The gradient is positive, then zero, then negative.

**Velocity-time:** a **straight line** of constant negative gradient, starting at $+u$, crossing zero at the top of the flight, and reaching $-u$ on being caught.

The area above the axis equals the area below, so the **total displacement is zero** — while the total **distance** is twice the height.

**Acceleration-time:** a **horizontal line** at $-g$ throughout, including at the very top.

**The point students find hardest:** at the highest point the velocity is zero but the acceleration is **still $g$**.

If the acceleration were zero there, the ball would stop and hang in mid-air. It is momentarily at rest and still being pulled downwards — which is precisely why it comes back.

questions.q: Explain, in terms of forces, why an object falling through air reaches a terminal velocity, and sketch in words its velocity-time graph.
questions.solution:
**At the moment of release.** The only force is the weight $mg$, so the acceleration is $g$ — the greatest it will ever be.

**As the speed increases.** Air resistance grows with speed (roughly as $v^{2}$ for a large object). The resultant force

$F = mg - R$

gets smaller, so the object is still speeding up, but **less and less rapidly**.

**At terminal velocity.** Air resistance has grown until $R = mg$. The resultant force is **zero**, so by Newton's first law the object continues at **constant velocity**.

It is not that the forces have stopped acting — they are balanced.

**The velocity-time graph.** A curve starting at the origin with gradient $g$, becoming progressively shallower, and levelling off asymptotically at the terminal velocity. The gradient is the acceleration, and it falls to zero without the velocity ever falling at all.

**A skydiver in practice.** Terminal velocity is about $55$ m/s spread-eagled, and up to $90$ m/s head-down, since $R$ depends on the area presented.

**Opening the parachute** increases $R$ enormously, so for a while $R > mg$ and the resultant force is **upwards** — the diver **decelerates**, settling at a new, much lower terminal velocity of about $5$ m/s.

The same analysis explains why a raindrop does not arrive at lethal speed, and why dust hangs in the air.

questions.q: Explain what is meant by relative velocity, and find the velocity of a boat that heads north at $4$ m/s across a river flowing east at $3$ m/s.
questions.solution:
**Relative velocity** is the velocity of one object as measured by an observer moving with another:

$\mathbf{v}_{AB} = \mathbf{v}_{A} - \mathbf{v}_{B}$

**The boat.** Its velocity relative to the water is $4$ m/s north; the water's velocity relative to the bank is $3$ m/s east. The boat's velocity relative to the **bank** is the vector sum:

$v = \sqrt{4^{2} + 3^{2}} = \mathbf{5}$ m/s

**Direction:** $\tan\theta = \dfrac34$, so $\theta = 36.9°$ **east of north**.

**What this means in practice.** The boat points north but travels north-east, and lands downstream of the point opposite.

**A striking consequence:** the time to cross depends **only** on the $4$ m/s northward component. A river $80$ m wide takes $20$ s whatever the current — the flow carries the boat sideways without delaying it at all.

**To land directly opposite**, the boat must head **upstream** at an angle, so that the westward component of its heading cancels the current.

That crossing takes longer, because part of the boat's speed is being spent fighting the river rather than crossing it.
